114.0.s.en: (1) The plots of the wicked against the righteous

114.0.0.en: 1- When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language, 2- Judah was his sanctuary, and Israel his dominion.

114.0.2.en: 1- The psalm shows that when the people of Israel went out of Egypt, and then took possession of the Promised Land, the tribe of Judah, in which Jerusalem and the temple are situated, was the holy place of God; for in Judah worship was offered in the temple, which was the holiest place in the world at that time. And they worshiped God and thanked Him because He brought them out of Egypt with great power by the ten plagues, from among a people who spoke a language strange to them. By Judah is meant not only the great tribe of Judah in which the temple stood, but the whole kingdom of the children of Israel, because God dwells in their midst.

114.0.3.en: 2- By Israel also is meant the whole kingdom of the children of Israel, and not only the ten tribes. The authority and power of God appeared in settling His people in the place of the wicked Canaanites in a land flowing with milk and honey, and in His protecting them from the surrounding nations when they held fast to Him, as in the days of David and Solomon. God's authority and protection are bound up with the submission of His people to Him and their holding fast to His commandments and Law. In sum, the people of God enjoy holiness and God's protection of them as long as they worship Him faithfully in His temple and live by His commandments.

114.1.0.en: "The sea saw it, and fled: Jordan was driven back."

114.1.1.en: 1- God's authority over nature appears in the fleeing of the waters of the sea before the power of God represented in the rod of Moses, so the sea was divided and the children of Israel crossed over. The river Jordan also turned back, to make a way for the people of God to cross into the land of Canaan. These two events, at two different times, represent God's authority over nature for the benefit of His people.

114.1.2.en: 2- The sea is a symbol of the world, of evil and of the demons, all of which flee before God, and the river is a symbol of the love of material things, which retreats before the believer's love for God; indeed the river is also a symbol of death, which retreated before the authority of God who rose from the dead, and before the saints who raised the dead. In sum, the believer in Christ has authority over nature, the demons and all evil if he holds fast to God.

114.2.0.en: "The mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs."

114.2.2.en: 1- The mountains and the little hills are the greatest things on earth, and they are firm and solid, yet they move before God and skip like rams and lambs, and tremble before the power of God, as the mountain quaked when God appeared on it to Moses and to all the people of Israel, when He gave Moses the commandments and the Law (Ex 19:18). The mountains also move before the power of God in His children, as Mount Mokattam was moved by the prayer of Simon the Tanner with the Pope and the people.

114.2.3.en: 2- The mountains are a symbol of the saints, such as the prophets and the Apostles, and all the saints who rejoice and skip with all their hearts praising God. And when the prophets and the Apostles moved from place to place proclaiming the word of God, they were like one who skips before God in zeal to declare His voice.

114.2.4.en: If God has all authority over the world, do not be troubled by changes in nature, or by the power of the rulers and the mighty of the world; all of them are in the grasp of God, the Ruler of all, and He moves them for your benefit if you hold fast to your faith and to God's commandments and His worship.

114.3.0.en: 5- What ailed thee, O thou sea, that thou fleddest? thou Jordan, that thou wast driven back? 6- Ye mountains, that ye skipped like rams; and ye little hills, like lambs? The writer of the psalm marvels at the mighty authority of God over nature, so that the seas and rivers flee and fear Him, and the mountains and hills also move as if they were children in their father's hands, for lambs are the young of the sheep and the rams. And he asks nature the reason for this movement of hers, and she answers only that she is subject to her God and Creator. This repetition, which was mentioned in (vv. 3, 4), is a confirmation of the greatness of God and His authority.

114.4.0.en: 7- Tremble, thou earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob; 8- Which turned the rock into a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters.

114.4.1.en: Standing water: pools, that is, a small river.

114.4.2.en: Flint: a very hard rocky stone called granite.

114.4.3.en: 1- Here the writer of the psalm answers his question in (vv. 5, 6): that nature, when she saw the fearful Lord, trembled. The Lord is the God of Jacob, so the earth trembled before the people of God when the Lord appeared on the mountain to Moses, as we mentioned. It also trembled when the archangel Michael announced the resurrection of the Lord Jesus from the dead. And in the wilderness of Sinai, when Moses struck the rock, it poured forth water like a river, and the people drank and glorified God (Num 20:11).

114.4.4.en: 2- These verses are a symbol of the trembling of man before the power of God in Baptism, when the old man dies and the new man is born, and then rivers of living water flow from his belly by the Holy Spirit.

114.4.5.en: And man's heart had been hardened by sin, but by faith it recovers its vitality, and indeed the Holy Spirit pours out of it the waters of grace, so that it is satisfied and satisfies others, for he is transformed into a light for the world and salt for the earth.

114.4.6.en: The Holy Spirit is ready to work in your heart however great your sins, so that your heart is softened and you are bound to the love of Christ, and are satisfied with Him, and indeed overflow upon others with giving and generosity.

114.4.7.en: The living God and the dead idols "Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory ..." (v. 1) Introduction:

114.4.8.en: 1- Its author: unknown, for there is no title for this psalm, and it is considered one of the orphan psalms whose author is unknown. There are many opinions about the author of this psalm; some think that he is:

114.4.14.en: 2- When was it written? It could be in one of the earlier times, that is, the days of Moses, or David, or during the captivity. Some think that it was written after the return from the captivity to be prayed in the temple as an encouragement to the returning Jews.

114.4.15.en: 3- There is a similarity between this psalm and the one before it in that they both speak of God who is able to do all things, and who protects His people and blesses them.

114.4.16.en: 4- There is a relation between this psalm and the psalm that follows it, in that this psalm asks for God's help, relies on Him and calls for His praise, whereas in the next psalm the victorious people of God praise Him.

114.4.17.en: 5- It is fitting for everyone in affliction to take refuge in God by repeating this psalm, and to rely on Him.

114.4.18.en: 6- This psalm is fitting for the children of God when they are exposed to affliction, so that they rely on God and ask for His blessing, that He may give them victory over their enemies.

114.4.19.en: 7- This psalm is considered liturgical, for the people used to chant it in alternation with the Levites and priests.

114.4.20.en: 8- Parts of this psalm, namely (vv. 16-18), are prayed in the funeral services of men and women, because they express the importance of praise throughout life.

114.4.21.en: 9- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.

115.0.0.en: "Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy, and for thy truth's sake."

115.0.1.en: 1- The writer of the psalm declares in humility his unworthiness of any grace or blessing because of the multitude of his sins.

115.0.2.en: 2- He shows that the reason for God's care and concern for His people is due to two things:

115.0.3.en: a - His limitless mercy toward all men, and especially His believing children.

115.0.4.en: b - His faithfulness in His fatherhood and His promises to His people.

115.1.0.en: "Wherefore should the heathen say, Where is now their God? But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased."

115.1.1.en: 1- The Gentiles cast doubt on the existence and power of God for the children of God, as Rabshakeh the Assyrian did to King Hezekiah (Isa 36:18-20; 37:1-13), and more dangerous still is for a man to doubt, within himself, the power of God. All these are attempts of Satan to separate us from God, so that we do not enjoy His protection of us.

115.1.2.en: And he also makes us doubt by saying that He is in heaven, far from us, and does not feel for us.

115.1.3.en: 2- (v. 3) declares the truth of the faith of God's children in Him, that our God is strong and rises above all creatures on earth, and is able to do all things, so He does what He pleases, and therefore He is able to protect His people. This is what the prophet Isaiah reassured King Hezekiah with, and the angel of God killed the army of Sennacherib, and the rest fled (Isa 37:33-38).

115.1.4.en: Meditation on the greatness of God and His power, and His many works with His children, and even in our own lives, establishes our faith, so that we are not disturbed by the changes of life or the false doubts of Satan.

115.2.0.en: "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands."

115.2.1.en: 1- These idols which the pagans worship, whether images, or statues made of stone and wood, or even made of silver and gold, are all the work of men's hands, and therefore they are not gods but things made by men, and are less than any creature that God created.

115.2.2.en: 2- The idols in our life now are what we cling to in life of material things, such as money, possessions and relationships .. and all of them pass away.

115.2.3.en: 3- The images of the saints, made of silver or gold or any material, are holy, because their subjects had holy lives, and we remember them by these images in order to honor them for the sake of God, for whom they lived faithfully, and to imitate them, and this gladdens God's heart.

115.3.0.en: "They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not: They have ears, but they hear not: noses have they, but they smell not: They have hands, but they handle not: feet have they, but they walk not: neither speak they through their throat."

115.3.1.en: The idols are portrayed in the form of men or animals, but they are far weaker and baser than they: though they have the form of mouths, they are unable to speak, and they have the form of eyes but are unable to see, and the look of ears does not give them the ability to hear, and though they have noses, they cannot smell. And though they have the form of hands and feet, they are unable to touch or walk, and they do not speak though they have throats; the smallest animal is able to make sounds, or walk, or make movements that the idols are unable to make, so of course they cannot be gods.

115.4.0.en: "They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them."

115.4.1.en: 1- If the idols are helpless, weak and base, then everyone who clings to them, whether he who makes them or worships them and trusts in them, becomes like them, weak and base, and indeed passing away like them, and becomes hard of heart like these stone idols. Thus man is degraded and separated from God by the worship of idols.

115.4.2.en: 2- On the contrary, he who worships God becomes like Him in purity, love, perfection, holiness and immortality.

115.4.3.en: Do not cling to the passing material things of the world and its desires, lest they take your heart captive and enslave you and take you away from God. You are greater than they, so use them for the glory of God, and your God is able to provide them for you as much as you need them.

115.5.0.en: "O Israel, trust thou in the LORD: he is their help and their shield. O house of Aaron, trust in the LORD: he is their help and their shield. Ye that fear the LORD, trust in the LORD: he is their help and their shield."

115.5.1.en: Their shield: the shield is the large buckler. It is a defensive instrument consisting of a piece of wood with a handle behind, into which the soldier puts his hand and moves it before his head and body to protect him from arrows.

115.5.2.en: 1- The writer of the psalm calls all the people of God to trust in Him, because He is their help in all their afflictions, and defends them before their enemies, so that they triumph over them. And he singles out especially the priests and servants when he says "house of Aaron," and then he affirms that God is the help and defender of those who fear the Lord, that is, who fear Him; meaning that all the people of God are called to trust in Him, and the priests and servants even more, and then the one who enjoys God's help and defense more than all is he who fears Him and reveres Him.

115.5.3.en: 2- Some interpreters think that those who fear the Lord are the Gentiles who feared God and believed in Him and joined His people; these God helps and defends like His people, and even more than His people, in proportion to their fear and faith in Him.

115.5.4.en: 3- God is the helper of His children in every generation in their wars against the demons, and He is also their defender, so He repels many attacks against them without their feeling it, and increases His protection of those who serve Him, and above all those who fear Him and revere Him, so that they live in peace and tranquility however great the wars of the demons.

115.5.5.en: Trust in the Lord is the ship in which we cross the sea of this world, however high its waves and strong its winds, so that inside the ship you enjoy fellowship with God, who protects us. And although we see with our eyes the wars of the demons, they are unable to hinder us from God, and indeed God uses them for our spiritual growth.

115.6.0.en: "The LORD hath been mindful of us: he will bless us; he will bless the house of Israel; he will bless the house of Aaron. He will bless them that fear the LORD, both small and great. The LORD shall increase you more and more, you and your children."

115.6.1.en: 1- God loves His people and remembers them because they are always in His thought, so He blesses them, as He gives a special blessing to His servants who are the house of Aaron, and above all to those who fear Him, whether of the Jews or of the Gentiles joined to them. And He increases His blessing to them, and also to their children, to gladden the hearts of the fathers; for our God is generous in giving and blessing, and His generosity is in proportion to His children's holding fast to His commandments, their fear of Him, and their love which appears in their service of His holy name.

115.6.2.en: 2- God remembers His children even if they are few and weak, as they were during the captivity, or at their return from the captivity, so He blesses them and increases their number and strength. So also in their wars with their enemies, as it was with Gideon, Jephthah and Samson in the age of the Judges, and as it was with David and Solomon, and also in the days of the Maccabees. And still to this day He protects His Church and blesses her with His power however few the believers in Him may be, but they are strong by His strength. For He blesses and increases everyone who fears Him, small and great, and indeed cares for the weak who rely on Him more than for the rest.

115.6.3.en: 3- The priest used to repeat these three great verses when offering the sacrifices in the tabernacle of meeting, or the temple of Solomon, so that the blessing would embrace all the people, and especially the priests and servants and those who fear the Lord.

115.7.0.en: "Ye are blessed of the LORD which made heaven and earth."

115.7.1.en: This blessing which God gives to His children affects them and draws them to love Him, so they are blessed of the Lord, and live for Him and worship Him faithfully and thank Him, and indeed serve Him with all their hearts, especially since they believe that their God has everything in His hand because He is the Creator of all, heaven and earth. And Melchizedek mentioned this blessing to Abraham when he blessed him, declaring that the blessing was for him from God, Creator of heaven and earth, that is, He in whose hand are all blessings (Gen 14:19).

115.8.0.en: "The heaven, even the heavens, are the LORD's: but the earth hath he given to the children of men. The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence. But we will bless the LORD from this time forth and for evermore. Praise the LORD."

115.8.1.en: 1- God is the Creator of heaven and earth, and He is exalted above all things; therefore the writer of the psalm expresses God's loftiness by saying that He dwells in heaven, and He created the first man in Paradise, but after the fall He gave him an opportunity to live on the earth, to show his faithfulness and his love for God, so that He may bring him back to heaven, where he enjoys freedom with the angels in fellowship with God and praises Him forever.

115.8.2.en: 2- The earth is an opportunity for the believing man to live with God and praise Him, not only with his tongue but with his heart and his good works; for he whose life ends and who dies and goes down to Hades (the land of silence), as used to happen in the Old Testament, has no opportunity to praise or to do good works.

115.8.3.en: 3- Those who live on earth while dead in sins do not praise God, nor live for Him, and so they lose His blessing which helps them to live with Him, and consequently do not reach the heavens.

115.8.4.en: Thank God every day for His blessings and His help and His protection of you, and lift up your heart in praise of Him, so that you taste the sweetness of fellowship with Him, until you come nearer every day to the life of the angels and the blessings of heaven.

115.8.5.en: Thanksgiving to God the Savior "I love the LORD, because he hath heard my voice and my supplications" (v. 1) Introduction:

115.8.6.en: 1- Its author: unknown, because the psalm has no title, so it is considered one of the orphan psalms.

115.8.7.en: But there is an opinion that its author is the prophet David.

115.8.8.en: 2- When was it written? If David is its author, he wrote it during, or after, his flight from the pursuit of Saul, or the pursuit of his son Absalom.

115.8.9.en: 3- This psalm is considered a psalm of thanksgiving to God, fitting for every believing man who passes through affliction, or whose affliction has ended, so that he praises God.

115.8.10.en: 4- The previous psalm (Ps 115) speaks in the spirit of the congregation with God, whereas this psalm speaks in the singular, and this makes it more affecting to the soul.

115.8.11.en: 5- This psalm is Messianic, because it speaks of the sufferings of Christ, His death and His victory.

115.8.12.en: 6- This psalm is liturgical, because it is used in worship in the Church of the New Testament, since the first part of it (vv. 1-9) is prayed in the funeral service of men.

115.8.13.en: 7- In the Septuagint translation this psalm is divided into two psalms (vv. 1-9), (vv. 10-19).

115.8.14.en: 8- This psalm is found in the prayers of the Agpeya in the prayer of the Ninth Hour, because it speaks of the sufferings of Christ, His death, and His victory over Satan, whom He bound by the cross at this hour.
